name: Stokes' law
seoTitle: Stokes' law Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Stokes' law: work out particle diameter (d) from the acceleration of gravity and the medium viscosity. A free physics calculator with the formula, units…
summary: particle diameter (d) is what the Stokes' law calculator works out, and it gets there from the acceleration of gravity, the medium viscosity, the medium density and the particle density. Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Stokes' law calculator work?
sections.html:
The Stokes' law calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports particle diameter (d) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the acceleration of gravity (g), the medium viscosity (μ), the medium density (ρ_m) and the particle density (ρ_p).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Stokes' law calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Particle diameter (d)=3 × the square root of (2) × the square root of (-terminal velocity (v) × medium viscosity (μ) ÷ (acceleration of gravity (g) × (medium density (ρ_m) − particle density (ρ_p))))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in millimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Acceleration, opening in meters per second squared
  • Viscosity – dynamic, opening in pascal seconds
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Speed, opening in meters per second

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Stokes' law calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the acceleration of gravity, the medium viscosity and the medium density — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Stokes' law calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns particle diameter (d), derived from the acceleration of gravity, the medium viscosity and the medium density. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Stokes' law calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the acceleration of gravity, the medium viscosity, the medium density and the particle density, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter acceleration of gravity (g) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Acceleration of gravity (g) opens in meters per second squared and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Stokes' law calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
